sections.h2: Selling a house in Leesburg and Lee County
sections.html:
Lee County has grown quickly, from 28,298 people in 2010 to an estimated 34,179 in mid-2025, on 355.88 square miles of land. Leesburg holds both tax offices, so most paperwork for a sale starts there.

Owners live in 74.2 percent of the county's 13,411 housing units, and the middle home is valued at $231,800. Median household income is $89,168, and the typical trip to work takes 23.1 minutes. Builders pulled 94 permits in 2025. Buyers with that kind of income read a tax bill closely, so have the latest copy ready.

Costs run above the neighboring counties. Lee owners pay a median $1,605 a month with a mortgage and $532 without, against $1,184 for renters. There are 12,287 households averaging 2.66 people, and 88.1 percent of residents stayed in the same house for a year. Most Lee owners stay put, so a seller who documents taxes and exemptions stands out. Bring the last bill, the deed and any exemption letter to the first meeting with your closing attorney.

Both offices are in Leesburg. The commissioner neither sets values nor sets rates.

Three board members serve three year terms by appointment of the county commissioners, and the board picks the chief appraiser. The board meets on the second Monday of each month at 4:30 p.m. in the Leslie Highway office. The county site links to online property records and a request form for withholding records from public view.

sections.h2: Due dates and how payments count
sections.html:
December 20 is the general due date. A mailed payment counts on a USPS postmark, and a postage meter stamp does not, so mail early. You can also pay online.

Interest and penalties after that date follow O.C.G.A. 48-2-40 and 48-2-44. A parcel left unpaid can be levied upon and sold.

Lee has issued refund checks to the owner of record on January 1 rather than to mortgage or escrow companies. A buyer who closed afterward should check the closing papers for any share, because the commissioner will not divide a check between the two parties. If escrow paid your bill, pass the refund to your servicer so it can be credited back. Escrow customers can ask the assessors for a letter to send their servicer, and a complaint about how refunds are issued belongs with your county commissioner.

Lee appraisers look at recent sales and conditions on January 1, and notices usually go out in spring. Appeal in writing to the board within 45 days of the notice date, and say how you want it heard.

The case can go to the Board of Equalization and then Superior Court, or to arbitration. The appeal cannot be about the amount of tax levied. Returns go to the board from January 1 through April 1. Keep your notice, because it states how to file and holds the date your 45 days start from. If the board changes your value after you file a return of your own, that return is what keeps your appeal open. Standing timber is taxed only when sold or cut, at 100 percent of market value. For value questions, ring 229-759-6010.

sections.h2: Exemptions you can claim or pass along
sections.html:
Lee adds local exemptions to the state set, and whichever amount is larger controls. The application goes to the Tax Assessor's Office, due April 1.

  • First-time owners bring a copy of the warranty deed.
  • Your driver's license has to show a physical Lee County address, because a post office box is refused.
  • Once granted, it carries forward until you change residence or ownership.

The county's tax page prints the whole menu, from the $2,000 standard exemption through elderly school and general exemptions, disabled veteran relief, a floating exemption and a deferral program, each with income limits. Brownfield sites can have their value frozen for a decade, and manufacturers apply for Freeport before April 1.

sections.h2: Who owes the tax in the year you sell
sections.html:
The January 1 owner, because no part-year refund exists in Georgia. Your closing attorney divides the bill.

  • Phone 229-759-6015 to see whether this year's bill is out and paid.
  • Request a payoff for any open balance.
  • Tell the buyer to file a fresh homestead application, because yours ends with your ownership.

If timber stood on your land, file the county's timber sale or harvest report, which both office pages link to. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal, but the payoff, the title search and the recorded deed work the same way.

File with the Board of Tax Assessors between January 1 and April 1, the same window as the homestead deadline. A real property return renews each year at the value set the year before, so a second filing is needed only after you add property, build or want to declare a new figure. Personal property returns must be refiled every year.

Owners who disagree with the board's number can declare a different one on a new return, which opens the appeal process if the board does not accept it. Call the assessors at 229-759-6010 for forms. A seller who has just built or added property should file in the same window, so the record matches the house a buyer sees.

sections.h2: Before you list a Lee County house
sections.html:
A little preparation shortens the closing. Put these in one folder before you meet your closing attorney: the latest tax bill, the deed, any exemption letter, your last assessment notice and any appeal paperwork. Lee County buyers tend to have strong household income, and they will ask what the yearly bill runs.

Call the commissioner at 229-759-6015 to confirm this year's bill is out and paid and to request a payoff for anything open. Call the assessors at 229-759-6010 to check your exemption and the property record. The county site has online property records you can search yourself, and a request form exists if you want records withheld from public view.

Plan on the mail too. Send any paper payment well before the due date, because only a USPS postmark counts, and keep the receipt. If your mortgage company pays through escrow, ask whether it received the bill, since notices follow the owner and the lender may not see them.

When a Lee County sale closes in spring, the January 1 owner is still responsible for the whole year, so the contract should say how the buyer reimburses you. Your closing attorney will handle the split, but you set the terms when you sign.

faqs.q: Where do I pay my Lee County tax bill?
faqs.a: At the commissioner's office, 100 Starksville Avenue North in Leesburg, by mail to P.O. Box 9, or online on the Lee tax site.

faqs.q: Does a postage meter stamp count on a Lee payment?
faqs.a: No. Lee accepts a United States Postal Service postmark only. Mail early or pay online.

faqs.q: Who receives a Lee County refund check on a house that sold?
faqs.a: The owner of record on January 1. The commissioner does not split checks, so buyer and seller settle it themselves.

faqs.q: What do first-time Lee homeowners bring to file a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: A copy of the warranty deed and a driver's license showing the Lee County address.

faqs.q: Can I appeal a Lee value only because my tax rose?
faqs.a: No. The appeal must rest on taxability, value or uniformity, or a denied exemption, filed within 45 days of the notice.
